title: Escape Velocity & Surface Gravity
theory: Escape = barely reaching infinity with zero speed: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{GMm}{R} = 0$. With surface gravity $g = GM/R^2$ (so $GM = gR^2$), this becomes the exam-ready $v_{esc} = \sqrt{2gR}$. Between planets, $v_{esc} \propto \sqrt{M/R}$.
framework: Energy at surface = energy at infinity (= 0).
Swap $GM \leftrightarrow gR^2$ to match the option set.
For ratios, cancel constants before any arithmetic.

problems.title: Escape speed in terms of g and R

parts.parameters:
- Given: Earth radius $R$, surface gravity $g$; object launched from the surface.
- Find: minimum speed to escape Earth's gravity.
parts.conclusion: "launched horizontally" is a distractor — escape *energy* is direction-blind (ignoring rotation/atmosphere). Option (a) $\sqrt{gR}$ is the surface circular-orbit speed; escape is $\sqrt{2}$ times it. Know the pair.

problems.title: Mass of the Earth from g and G

parts.conclusion: convert km → m **first** — the $10^{18}/10^{30}$ options exist purely to punish that slip. Two significant figures throughout.
≈ 11 km/s — a benchmark to cache. Option (e) $7.9\times10^3$ m/s is the low-orbit speed, the *other* famous number; knowing both makes the distractor flag itself.
pure ratio — $G$, $g$, radii in meters: none needed. Bracket the root: $\sqrt{25}=5 < \sqrt{29.1} < \sqrt{36}=6$, closer to 5.4. Bracketing beats long division under time pressure.
